cards.hearing: You may be hearing about tension in the Middle East, with reports that the U.S. is weighing new action on Iran and fighting flaring up between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. Oil prices moved up on that news.
cards.why: Oil is the raw material behind gas and diesel, so headlines like this can nudge what it costs to fill up the car or move goods on a truck.
cards.but: But a single week of oil news is not the same as a shift in your long-term plan.
cards.story: Picture a family road trip where gas costs more at one stop. You don't cancel the whole trip over one pump price, you just keep driving toward where you're headed.
say: We see the oil headline, and we keep driving toward your goals.
One pricier fill-up doesn't rewrite the whole trip.

cards.hearing: You may be hearing that a Fed official said more interest rate hikes could be needed, and that borrowing costs, like the rate on a 30-year mortgage, ticked up a little this week.
cards.why: When voices at the Fed, which sets short-term interest rates, talk about raising rates, it can show up in things like mortgage payments or loan costs for a car or business.
cards.but: But your plan was built knowing interest rates would move around over time, not stay frozen.
cards.story: Picture a thermostat that gets bumped up or down in a house. The family doesn't call a meeting to sell the house every time the temperature shifts, they just adjust and keep living there.
say: Interest rate talk is normal noise, not a reason to redo the plan.
We built your plan expecting the thermostat to move.

cards.hearing: You may be hearing that stocks slipped a little this week, including yesterday, Wednesday, and that futures were a touch softer heading into today.
cards.why: Weeks like this can feel unsettling, but small wobbles in stocks are a normal part of investing, not a sign something is broken.
cards.but: But there's no major event behind this move, just ordinary day-to-day drift that markets do all the time.
cards.story: Picture someone who cancels their gym membership every time a week feels off, then restarts it a month later. They pay the signup fee again and again, but barely get any of the benefit. Staying invested is the market version of keeping the membership.
say: A quiet dip like this isn't a reason to step out.
We stay in through the dull weeks, not just the exciting ones.
